---
title: "Getting started"
subtitle: "An end-to-end analysis in about thirty lines"
---

## Install

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/ablack3/EmpyriCal.git
```

Or from a clone, for development:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ablack3/EmpyriCal.git
cd EmpyriCal
pip install -e ".[test]"
```

Requires Python 3.9+, with NumPy, SciPy, pandas and matplotlib.

## What you need to bring

Empirical calibration operates on **effect estimates that already exist**. This
package does not fit outcome models, build cohorts or touch a database — you run
your study, and bring back:

| | |
|---|---|
| `logRr` | the effect estimate on the **log** scale |
| `seLogRr` | its standard error, also on the log scale |

for your hypothesis of interest **and** for a set of negative controls run
through the identical pipeline. If your analysis reports a relative risk and a
95% confidence interval instead, convert:

```{python}
import numpy as np

rr, lb95 = 1.32, 1.05
logRr = np.log(rr)
seLogRr = (np.log(lb95) - np.log(rr)) / -1.959964   # qnorm(0.025)
print(f"logRr = {logRr:.4f}, seLogRr = {seLogRr:.4f}")
```

The packaged datasets have this shape:

```{python}
import empiricalcalibration as ec

sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
sccs.head()
```

`groundTruth` is 1 for the positive control and 0 for negative controls. Five
datasets ship with the package: `sccs`, `caseControl`, `cohortMethod`,
`southworthReplication` and `grahamReplication`.

## Step 1 — fit the null

```{python}
negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]
positive = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 1]

null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
print(null)
```

Before going further, look at it. A mean far from zero or a standard deviation
much above 0.1 says the design has substantial systematic error — worth knowing
regardless of what you do next.

```{python}
ease = ec.computeExpectedAbsoluteSystematicError(null)
print(f"EASE = {ease:.3f} (typical estimate off by a factor of {np.exp(ease):.2f})")
```

## Step 2 — calibrate the p-value

```{python}
p_trad = ec.computeTraditionalP(positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr)
p_cal = ec.calibrateP(null, positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr)

print(f"traditional p: {p_trad[0]:.4g}")
print(f"calibrated  p: {p_cal[0]:.4g}")
```

## Step 3 — calibrate the confidence interval

With only negative controls, promote the null into an error model under the
assumption that the error distribution is the same at every true effect size:

```{python}
model = ec.convertNullToErrorModel(null)
ci = ec.calibrateConfidenceInterval(positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr, model)

trad = ec.computeTraditionalCi(positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr)
print(f"traditional: RR {trad.rr.iloc[0]:.2f} "
      f"({trad.lb.iloc[0]:.2f} - {trad.ub.iloc[0]:.2f})")
print(f"calibrated:  RR {np.exp(ci.logRr.iloc[0]):.2f} "
      f"({np.exp(ci.logLb95Rr.iloc[0]):.2f} - {np.exp(ci.logUb95Rr.iloc[0]):.2f})")
```

That assumption is doing real work — see
[the warning](../methods/confidence-intervals.qmd#when-you-only-have-negative-controls).
If you have positive controls, fit the error model properly instead:

```python
model = ec.fitSystematicErrorModel(data.logRr, data.seLogRr, data.trueLogRr)
```

## Step 4 — look at it

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Negative controls (blue) and the positive control (yellow) against the fitted empirical null."
fig = ec.plotCalibrationEffect(
    negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr,
    positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr,
    showExpectedAbsoluteSystematicError=True,
)
```

Every plot returns a `matplotlib.figure.Figure`, so you can adjust it or save it
however you like. Passing `fileName=` saves directly, at the R package's
dimensions:

```python
fig = ec.plotCalibrationEffect(..., fileName="calibration.png")
```

## The whole thing

```python
import empiricalcalibration as ec

null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
model = ec.convertNullToErrorModel(null)

p = ec.calibrateP(null, study.logRr, study.seLogRr)
ci = ec.calibrateConfidenceInterval(study.logRr, study.seLogRr, model)
ease = ec.computeExpectedAbsoluteSystematicError(null)
```

## How many negative controls?

Fifty or so is the working guidance from the OHDSI studies. Below about twenty
the fitted null is unstable enough that calibration adds as much noise as it
removes — see
[the simulation](../methods/null-distribution.qmd#what-the-number-of-controls-buys-you).
If you are stuck with few controls, use [`fitMcmcNull`](../methods/mcmc.qmd) so
the resulting uncertainty is at least visible in the output.

## Reproducibility

Stochastic functions draw from a port of R's Mersenne-Twister, so `ec.set_seed`
reproduces R's `set.seed` streams exactly:

```{python}
ec.set_seed(42)
a = ec.simulateControls(n=5, mean=0.2, sd=0.2, trueLogRr=0)
ec.set_seed(42)
b = ec.simulateControls(n=5, mean=0.2, sd=0.2, trueLogRr=0)
print("identical:", np.array_equal(a.logRr.values, b.logRr.values))
```
